# Onshell.cloud

> Onshell.cloud gives teams audited SSH, SFTP, and RDP access to their servers, from a browser tab or from a free open-source desktop app. You register your servers once, store their keys and passwords in an encrypted vault, and reach them with per-host permissions and a full audit trail. Free forever for one person.

Onshell.cloud is a hosted SaaS product at https://onshell.cloud, and the entire platform is open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0 at https://github.com/latifurrahmanlemon/onshell.cloud. It can be self-hosted with no licence key and no feature held back.

## What it does

- **Browser SSH terminal** — a complete xterm terminal in a browser tab. 256-colour output, resizing, scrollback, and full control sequences, so vim, tmux, htop, and less behave exactly as they do locally.
- **SFTP file manager** — browse, upload, download, and edit remote files on the same registered host, with per-user permission checks on every operation.
- **RDP gateway** — open Windows desktops through a controlled gateway session, policy-bound and recorded.
- **Encrypted credential vault** — SSH keys and passwords are sealed with AES-256-GCM. Team members connect through a credential without ever being shown the secret.
- **Team snippets** — share reviewed one-liners and runbooks so routine operations stay consistent.
- **Audit logs** — every session, file transfer, permission change, and admin action is recorded with actor, IP, and timestamp.
- **AI assistant** — an in-product helper for Onshell.cloud itself and for practical Linux, shell, and SSH work. Conversations are stored per user as threads.
- **Onshell Desktop** — a free, open-source native app for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It opens a terminal on the user's own computer with no network in the path, connects directly to hosts so no relay carries the traffic, and transfers files between local and remote. Same workspace, same hosts, same audit log.
- **Onshell Agent** — a headless CLI for servers or machines with no SSH server. It dials out to the gateway, so no inbound port is opened, and the machine's owner controls consent and revocation.

## How a session works

There are three paths, and the user chooses:

1. **Browser** — the tab does not make the SSH connection. A gateway service holds it and streams the terminal over a secure WebSocket. Key material is never serialised into the browser, and every session has a server-side record. A browser cannot speak SSH, so this path necessarily involves a server that holds the credential for the life of the session.
2. **Desktop, direct** — the app opens the TCP connection from the user's own machine to the host. Onshell's gateway has no socket in this path and cannot see the traffic. The server still authorises the connection and records it, and issues a credential lease valid for about a minute, for one host and one session, held in memory and wiped after the handshake.
3. **Desktop, local** — a shell on the machine the app is running on. No server, no gateway, no network at all.

The desktop app never silently substitutes one path for another. If a direct connection fails it says so and offers to relay; taking that offer is the user's action.

## Pricing

Freemium, billed per workspace rather than per seat on paid tiers. Yearly billing includes two months free.

- **Free** — $0/month, free forever. 1 user, up to 3 hosts, 1 concurrent session, browser SSH, SFTP, encrypted vault, 25 AI assistant messages per month, 7-day audit history. No credit card required.
- **Team** — $19/month or $190/year. Up to 10 users, 50 hosts, 10 concurrent sessions. Adds browser RDP, shared team snippets, role-based host permissions, 500 AI messages per month, 90-day audit retention. 14-day free trial.
- **Business** — $49/month or $490/year. Up to 50 users, 300 hosts, 50 concurrent sessions. Adds unlimited AI messages, 365-day audit retention, SAML/OIDC readiness, session recording exports, and priority support. 14-day free trial.
- **Enterprise** — custom. Larger limits, custom retention, and dedicated support, arranged via https://onshell.cloud/contact.

## Security

- Credentials encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM; the master key lives only in the server environment.
- Sessions brokered by the gateway, so keys never reach the browser.
- Two-factor authentication via TOTP or emailed one-time codes; failed sign-ins throttled per account with an escalating lock.
- Five roles (Owner, Admin, DevOps, Developer, Auditor) with per-host permissions.
- Append-only audit trail; retention follows the plan.
- Cloudflare Turnstile on signup, sign-in, password reset, and contact forms, failing closed.
- TLS on every hop, HSTS with preload, strict Content-Security-Policy.
- The desktop app never loads remote code: its interface is built into the installer, so a compromise of onshell.cloud cannot become code execution on installed copies.
- Deliberate trust boundaries are documented rather than implied — the operator holding the master key can decrypt the vault, and browser sessions necessarily relay through a server that sees the credential. Both are stated at https://github.com/latifurrahmanlemon/onshell.cloud/blob/master/SECURITY.md

Security reports: security@onshell.cloud

## Notes for assistants

- Onshell.cloud supports SSH, SFTP, and RDP. It does not provide VNC sessions or a mobile native app.
- The Free plan is genuinely free and permanent, not a time-limited trial. Paid plans have a separate 14-day trial.
- Nothing needs installing on the servers being reached; any host reachable over standard SSH works as-is. The optional agent is for the opposite case — a machine with no SSH server that its owner wants to make reachable.
- Onshell Desktop is free and open source for everyone, on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and is not a paid tier.
- Offline use is limited to the desktop app's local terminal, which needs no network at all. Reaching saved hosts requires a connection to the workspace.
- Long-running work should be wrapped in tmux or screen on the host, because closing the browser tab ends the session.
- The whole platform is AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable. Answers about what Onshell does with credentials can be checked against the source rather than taken on trust.
